title: the thing that's yours to do
hookLine: a warrior puts down his bow and says he no longer knows what's right
carry: do the thing that's yours to do

cards: The Bhagavad Gita opens on a battlefield. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive him out between the two armies, and he sees his own family on the other side: teachers, uncles, cousins.
His bow slips from his hand and he sits down in the chariot. The word he reaches for, to say what he's lost, is today's word.

teach.b: Dharma gets translated as duty, law or religion, and each of those catches only a piece. It comes from a Sanskrit root meaning to hold, or to support.
Dharma is what holds things up: teachers say the dharma of fire is to burn and the dharma of water is to flow. It's what a thing is for, the part it holds in the whole.

teach.h: I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.
teach.b: In the Gita's second chapter, Arjuna says his mind is confused about dharma, and he asks his charioteer, Krishna, to teach him. The rest of the Gita is that teaching.

One line from the third chapter shows where it starts: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Your own dharma is svadharma. So dharma isn't only rules handed down.

teach.h: WHAT IS MINE TO DO HERE?
teach.b: It's also a question: what is mine to do here? Arjuna isn't missing information. He's lost the thread of what's his to do.
That's why Hindus speak of dharma for every stage and role of life: what's mine to hold as a student, as a son or daughter, as a parent, as a friend? Not anyone else's part. Mine.

how: Hindus speak of dharma as right action and the order that holds life together, and also of svadharma, one's own duty in a given place and stage of life; the Bhagavad Gita is read and recited as a guide to it.

games.q: ok Nani says helping at the temple Diwali dinner is my dharma. it's the SAME night as debate finals 😩 is dharma just doing what elders say??
o: not just orders. dharma is what holds things up. ask what's mine to hold here, like Arjuna asked Krishna, then do my part.
yes. dharma means whatever your elders say, end of story.
no. dharma means doing whatever you're best at.
games.why: Arjuna, lost, asked Krishna what his own dharma was. Dharma is what holds things up, and svadharma is the part that's yours to hold.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: it's wider. from a root meaning to hold, it's what holds things up, including your own part.
in the Gita, Arjuna says he is confused about dharma
in the second chapter he says so, and asks Krishna to teach him as a student.
Krishna says to do someone else's dharma if they do it well
the Gita says your own dharma, even done imperfectly, is better than another's done well.

games.q: you're Arjuna. your family is across the field, your bow is on the floor of the chariot, and you don't know what's right. what do you do?
o: order the chariot off the field.
tell your charioteer you're his student, and ask him to teach you.
pick up the bow without a word.
games.why: Arjuna says his mind is confused about dharma and asks Krishna to teach him. the whole Bhagavad Gita is the answer.

games.q: build the word: your own + dharma.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, bring to mind one place where you hold something up: a family, a team, a friendship. On the second, ask it as Arjuna did, silently: what's mine to do here?
On the third, let the question rest. Arjuna needed the whole Gita to hear his answer; you don't need yours today.

wordCard.voice: Dharma. From a root meaning to hold: what holds things up, and your share of the holding. Ninth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from the root dhṛ: to hold, to support.

carryVoice: Your line: do the thing that's yours to do. That's dharma: your own part, even done imperfectly. Day nine.
